title: Search inside a member community
metaTitle: Search that speaks a member's language
excerpt: Members search a community when the rooms and the feed fail them. Show matches in their words, keep the query visible, and give them a way back to where they were.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky, a dense set of rooms a member has to find a way through.
caption: When the streets all look alike, people ask for a name. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Why do members search instead of browsing rooms?
faqs.answer: They search because the navigation failed them. The feed ranked the thread out of sight, the room list uses internal names, or someone told them a phrase and they cannot find the door. Search is the repair for that miss. It is not a reward you unlock after they learn your map.

faqs.question: What should a community search result show?
faqs.answer: Show the kind of thing it is, in their words: a person, a room, or a post. Include the snippet that matched, the room the post lives in, and whether they can reply there. A row that is only an avatar and a title makes them open five wrong objects. The match should be visible before the tap.

faqs.question: What should happen when nothing matches?
faqs.answer: Repeat the query so they can see what produced nothing. Offer a smaller next step, such as searching rooms only, or posting the question in a room they can speak in. Do not replace the empty result with the entire feed. That hides the failure and makes them think the product ignored them.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Member community search UX starts from a failure you already shipped. A person deciding whether to post or lurk opens search when the rooms, the feed, or the notification did not get them to the thing they were promised. Show matches in their language, and show a way back.

They are not browsing for fun. They have a name, a phrase, or a room someone mentioned in passing. If the results are in your internal vocabulary, they will assume the thing does not exist. Then they will either post a duplicate or go quiet. Both are expensive, and both are avoidable with a result row that speaks plainly.

## Search is what happens after navigation fails

Treat search as the recovery path, not as a power feature for experts. The member who searches on day one is telling you the map failed. The feed hid the thread. The sidebar has forty rooms with clever names. The invite said "say hello in Welcome" and they cannot see Welcome.

Design the search entry so it is findable on a phone without a tour. A field in the header, or a single search tab, is enough. Do not bury it inside a menu labeled Explore. Explore is a second map. They already rejected the first one.

Keep the place they came from. If they were in a room and they search, they need a way back to that room even if they never tap a result. A search that replaces the room and offers no return makes the product feel like it ate their context. The back control should say the room's name, not only "Back."

Jakob Nielsen's note for the Nielsen Norman Group is that people often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is obvious immediately. A results screen is under the same pressure. The first results have to look like the thing they typed, in words they used, or they will leave the search and maybe the community. [How long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is a useful check on a results page that opens with filters, tips, and a featured post that does not match the query.

## Matches in their language

Index the words members actually say. Room names, people's names, and the text of posts. Also index the awkward versions: a first name only, a room's plain description, a phrase from the invite email. If the room is officially "Signal / Design Crit" and everyone calls it "crit," both should hit.

Group the results by the kind of object, with labels. People. Rooms. Posts. A single blended list sorted by a score they cannot see will put a member named Ada above the thread Ada wrote, or the reverse, with no explanation. Groups let them skip to the kind they meant.

Each post result needs the sentence that matched, the room, and the date in ordinary language. Highlight the matching words in the snippet. A title alone is not a match. They searched for a phrase because they do not know the title.

Each room result needs the one-line reason the room exists, plus whether they can reply. Sending them into a read-only room from search, with no warning, recreates the permission bug at the end of a successful search. The result row can say "Read only" before they open it.

Each person result needs the name they post under and the room they are active in, if you show activity at all. Do not show a private email. Do not show a member who has chosen not to appear in search. That choice belongs in settings, and search has to honor it without a leak in the snippet.

Skip internal ids, slug lines, and "relevance 0.82." None of that helps a person decide whether to post or keep lurking. If two posts are similar, show both snippets. Let them choose. A magical single hit that is wrong is worse than two honest ones.

## A way back, including back to the words they typed

The query stays on screen after they search. They will edit a word. They will delete a word. If you clear the field on submit, you have asked them to remember what they just typed, which is a strange tax.

Provide a clear control that empties the query and returns them to where they were. Provide a result tap that opens the object, and a return from that object to the same results, query intact. Losing the query on the way back is how a three-step lookup becomes a frustrated reload.

If they came from a notification and bounced into search, the way back might be the notification's thread, not a generic home. Home is a weak landmark in a community. The room is the landmark. Name it.

Recent searches can help on a return visit. Keep the list short, on the device or the account, and let them remove a line. A community search history that shows a sensitive question on a shared computer is a real harm. If you store it, make removing it obvious. If the product is used on shared phones, consider not storing it at all.

Do not "helpfully" replace their query with a corrected one without showing both. "Showing results for design" under a search for a person's name is how you hide a miss. If you have a correction, offer it as a separate line they can tap. Keep their words in the field until they accept yours.

## When nothing matches

Repeat the query in the empty state. "No posts contain 'pricing office hours.'" That sentence proves the product heard them. "No results" does not say for what.

Then offer a way forward that respects the post-or-lurk decision. Suggest rooms whose names are close. Offer to ask the question in a room they can post in, with the query carried into the composer so they do not retype it. Carrying the words is the difference between an empty state that helps and one that scolds.

Do not dump the whole feed under the empty message. The feed is how this person got lost. Filling the silence with unrelated posts looks like the search ignored them.

If the miss is because they lack permission to see the matching room, be careful. Saying "there is a private room you cannot see" can leak that the room exists. Saying "nothing you can open matches that" is the honest public version. Pick the policy with whoever runs the community, and write it down. Accidental leaks in empty states are a classic failure.

Spelling and partial names deserve a kind miss. "No member named Jordan Lee. Members named Jordan:" is useful. A hard empty on a one-character typo teaches people the directory is empty.

## What not to rank first

Do not rank a pinned announcement above a true match. Pins belong in the room. Search belongs to the query. A pinned code of conduct on every query trains people to ignore the first result, which then hurts the queries where the first result was right.

Do not lead with people when they clearly typed a question. A question mark, or a sentence, is a post lookup. A single token that matches a member name can lead with people and still show posts underneath. The grouping matters more than a clever score.

Do not boost the member's own unseen drafts into the list without labeling them as drafts. Finding your own unsent reply and thinking it was published is a nasty surprise. Label drafts as drafts, or leave them out of community search and find them in a Drafts list.

Filters are optional. A room filter helps after they have seen a mixed list and want to narrow it. A screen that demands a room, a date, and a type before it will search is a form, not a search. Default to the whole community they can access, then let them narrow.

## Review the search with a lost member

Write five lookups a new member will actually attempt. A host's first name. A room nickname from the invite. A phrase from a post they saw once. A question they want to ask, to see if it was already asked. A word that should miss.

Run them on a phone, as a member, not as an admin. Admin search that sees private rooms will pass tests members fail. For each lookup, you should be able to tell what matched, get back to the prior room, and still see the query.

Time the first result. If the screen spends its first moments on a skeleton of filters, you are spending the seconds in which they decide the community cannot find anything. Show rows as soon as you have them.

The cabinet beside search is where they control whether their name is findable and how loud the community is. That is the next piece, [settings in a member community](/blog/settings-in-a-member-community). Search that ignores those choices will feel like a breach even when the results are relevant.

If you want the recovery path designed with the same care as the happy path, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). A search box on a screenshot is not the feature. The feature is a match they recognize, and a way back if it is the wrong one.
